---
title: "Research Interests"
---

I am interested in how the brain builds reliable representations of the world
during development, and in particular in the part that the cortex's own internal
structure plays in this process.

## How the cortex prepares for seeing before it sees

Before eye opening, the visual cortex already shows richly structured
spontaneous activity. I want to understand what this endogenous structure is
good for: how it is shaped by recurrent connectivity, and how far it constrains
what the cortex can later learn from experience.

## How experience turns variable responses into reliable ones

At eye opening, responses to the same stimulus differ from trial to trial;
within days they become reliable. I am interested in the circuit mechanisms
behind this transition. Our work so far suggests that reliability emerges when
visual input becomes aligned with the pre-existing network structure, rather
than through a general reduction of noise. See
*Trägenap et al., Nature Neuroscience 2025*
([press release](https://fias.institute/en/news/news-publicity/learning-to-see-a-mix-of-nature-and-nurture/) ·
[free-to-read version](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-024-01857-3.epdf?sharing_token=GwWYQRrz-zub53Fug5n7UdRgN0jAjWel9jnR3ZoTv0M7mcLR7y-jFw14-nj_gtm6ywdvYoPVRIr_VUd7JsYV_8IKHS0hYLlzSCcrssR-rATJZeAwYyx6R5SJjIyj4cSPLALkqJbHibiN74JKVL2qsolm3CfkUvDI4TAUomlN-BQ%3D)).

## Feedforward input meets recurrent circuits

How do feedforward inputs and recurrent cortical circuits shape each other as
the cortex matures? With the Fitzpatrick lab we found that coherent cortical
responses develop as feedforward inputs become more discriminable and better
aligned with the recurrent network. See
*Lempel, Trägenap et al., Neuron 2025*
([press release](https://fias.institute/en/news/news-publicity/learning-to-see-is-teamwork/) ·
[doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2025.08.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.08.014)).

## Selective amplification across the cortical sheet

Which activity patterns does the developing cortex amplify, and which does it
suppress? With the Smith lab we study selective amplification on the scale of
millimetres and ask which recurrent subnetworks can account for it. See
*Mulholland, Trägenap et al., bioRxiv 2026* (co-first authors;
[doi:10.64898/2026.03.31.715687](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.31.715687)).

## Looking ahead: across the animal tree

Most of what we know about cortical development comes from a handful of species.
Yet brains differ, shaped by different evolutionary histories and different ways
of seeing the world. By comparing how the cortex is organised in ferrets, cats,
tree shrews and mice, I hope to tell apart the developmental principles that are
shared across species from those that are particular to one. Where a species
departs from the others, the departure itself points to the mechanism at work.

## Looking ahead: from biology to learning machines

The developing cortex solves a problem that artificial systems also face: how to
learn quickly from limited experience. I am curious whether the strategy we see in
the brain, starting from a structured prior and aligning input to it, could make
learning in artificial neural networks faster or more robust.

## Approach

I work at the interface of theory and experiment: dynamical recurrent network
models, analysis of large-scale calcium imaging data, and the comparison of
model predictions with chronically recorded neural populations. I enjoy working
closely with experimental partners and being part of the loop between theory
and experiment that drives science forward: a model can suggest what to measure,
and the measurement reshapes the model. In my PhD work I have collaborated with
the labs of David Fitzpatrick (Max Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience) and
Gordon Smith (University of Minnesota).
